blocks.text: It was now late in the afternoon, and sunset was not far away. We had to accept that our chase was over. With heavy hearts we agreed with the Professor when he said:—

“Let us go back to Madam Mina—poor, poor dear Madam Mina. We have done all that we can do just now. And there, at least, we can protect her. But we need not lose hope. There is only one more earth-box, and we must try to find it. When that is done, all may still be well.” I could see that he spoke as bravely as he could, to comfort Harker. The poor man was completely broken. Now and then he gave a low groan that he could not hold back. He was thinking of his wife.

With sad hearts we came back to my house. Mrs. Harker was waiting for us there. She looked cheerful, and this showed how brave and unselfish she was. When she saw our faces, her own face became as pale as death. For a second or two her eyes were closed, as if she were praying in secret. Then she said cheerfully:—

“I can never thank you all enough. Oh, my poor darling!” As she spoke, she took her husband’s grey head in her hands and kissed it. “Lay your poor head here and rest it. All will still be well, dear! God will protect us if He wishes it, in His good purpose.” The poor man groaned. His misery was so deep and so noble that there was no place for words in it.

We had a sort of supper together, though we ate without much interest. I think it cheered us all up a little. Perhaps it was only the simple bodily warmth of food for hungry people. None of us had eaten anything since breakfast. Or perhaps being together helped us. But anyway, we were all less miserable. We felt that tomorrow was not completely without hope. We kept our promise and told Mrs. Harker everything that had happened. At times she grew as white as snow, when danger had seemed to threaten her husband. At other times she grew red, when we told how much he loved her and how much he had done for her. But she listened bravely and calmly. Then we came to the part where Harker had rushed at the Count so wildly, without thinking of his own safety. She held on to her husband’s arm and gripped it tightly. It was as though her holding on could protect him from any harm that might come. However, she said nothing until we had told the whole story and brought it right up to the present time. Then, still holding her husband’s hand, she stood up among us and spoke. Oh, I wish I could give some idea of that scene! She was a sweet, sweet, good, good woman, shining and beautiful in her youth and liveliness. There was a red scar on her forehead, and she knew it was there. We saw it and ground our teeth, because we remembered where it had come from and how. Her loving kindness stood against our grim hate. Her gentle faith stood against all our fears and doubts. And we knew something terrible. As far as signs and symbols could show, she was an outcast from God, sent away from Him, even with all her goodness and purity and faith.

“Jonathan,” she said. The word sounded like music on her lips, because it was so full of love and tenderness. “Jonathan dear, and all of you, my true, true friends, I want you to remember something through all this terrible time. I know that you must fight. I know that you must destroy, just as you destroyed the false Lucy so that the true Lucy might live afterwards. But this is not a work of hate. That poor soul who has caused all this misery is the saddest case of all. Just think how happy he will be when his worse part is destroyed too. Then his better part may live forever in the spirit. You must feel pity for him too, even though your pity may not hold your hands back from destroying him.”

As she spoke, I could see her husband’s face grow dark and tight. It was as though the strong feeling in him were shrinking and drying up his whole being, right to its centre. Without thinking, he held his wife’s hand more and more tightly, until his knuckles looked white. I knew she must have felt pain, but she did not pull away from it. Instead she looked at him with eyes that begged him more strongly than ever. When she stopped speaking, he jumped to his feet. He almost tore his hand away from hers as he spoke:—
